Four verticals against Cover 3, simulated (BDB-format tracking, generated by gridiron). The cornerbacks bail with the outside receivers, staying two or three yards on top of them; the curl-flat defenders run with the seams for a few steps and then let them go; and the free safety (ringed) has to choose. The quarterback looks to his right as he drops (the green arrow is his eyes), and the safety drifts that way, toward Y; the ball goes to H on the left seam, behind the curl-flat defender and in front of the cornerback, about 25 yards downfield. The safety breaks on the throw, too late.
:::
:::


Notice what the quarterback did with his eyes. He looked toward Y as he dropped, and the safety,
who reads the quarterback, drifted that way. Moving a defender with your eyes is called a
[look-off](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-look-off), and it's an essential skill for any concept
that reads a single deep defender ([Quarterback Play](04-07-quarterback-play.qmd) has more).

Four verticals has no single inventor. Its roots are usually traced to the vertical passing games
of Sid Gillman and Don Coryell, to LaVell Edwards's BYU and to the
[run-and-shoot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-run-and-shoot) offenses of Mouse Davis, all of which
built their attacks around receivers running up the field; the Air Raid turned it into a signature
call, with receivers taught to stay in their lanes but get open in them.[^fourverts] In the modern
NFL it rarely looks like four straight lines. The seam runners usually carry a read, holding
straight against one deep safety and bending inside between two (a route conversion, as below), and
offenses with speed outside, like Andy Reid's Chiefs with Tyreek Hill, use the outside go routes to
push the cornerbacks off.

### Post-wheel

[**Post-wheel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-post-wheel) splits the defenders on one side,
inside and out. The outside receiver runs a post, angling toward the middle at about 12
yards; the inside receiver (or a back) runs a wheel, out toward the flat and then straight up the
sideline, into the space the post receiver just left. It is read high and outside first: the
wheel.

::: {#cell-fig-post-wheel .cell execution_count=19}
``` {.python .cell-code}
p = Play(spread(), cover3(nb_side=1), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
route_to(p, "Z", (10.0, 15.0), (19.5, 7.5))
route_to(p, "Y", (-0.8, 11.5), (1.5, 14.5), (5.5, 18.5), (21.0, 19.4))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("NB", (6.0, 13.6))
p.drop("FS", (16.0, 0.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0))
p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6))
p.highlight("RCB", "NB")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (21.0, 21.9)), (2, (21.2, 7.0)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (11.3, -15.0), (11.3, -5.0)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (20.0, -7.6)]],
            stretch="Horizontal stretch: corner and $",
            keys=["route", "ghost", "drop", "react", "num", "ring", "ltg"])
branch(fld, p, [(7.0, 16.0), (11.5, 15.6), (16.5, 11.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
say(fld, p, 13.5, 22.4, "wheel", color=OD)
say(fld, p, 12.4, 9.0, "post", color=OD)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Post-wheel to the offense's right against match Cover 3, a version many NFL defenses now play. Z runs a post; Y, from the slot, runs a wheel, out toward the flat and then up the sideline. The two ringed defenders are the pair in conflict. The cornerback's rule is to carry the outside receiver when he goes deep, so the post drags him inside (dashed). That hands the wheel to the nickel ($), the curl-flat defender, who widened with Y's release from five yards deep and can't turn and run with him up the sideline. Progression: (1) the wheel; (2) the post, if the cornerback passes Z on to the free safety and stays outside; (3) the back on the left. H's seam (grey) holds the free safety in the middle.](04-04-dropback-concepts_files/figure-html/fig-post-wheel-output-1.svg){#fig-post-wheel}
:::
:::


Why does it work? Because each defender on that side has a sensible rule, and the two routes make
the rules collide. Many NFL defenses now play *match* Cover 3: instead of dropping to a spot, each
defender picks up a receiver once the routes declare. The cornerback's rule is to carry the outside
receiver if he goes deep, so when Z pushes vertical and bends to the post, the cornerback goes
inside with him. The curl-flat defender's rule is to take the second receiver if he goes to the
flat. The wheel starts as exactly that, a harmless flat route, and then turns up the sideline,
where a nickel who started five yards deep, facing the quarterback, has to turn and run with a
receiver who already has a head of steam. The wheel is behind him and outside the cornerback,
and nobody's rule covers it in time.

If the cornerback refuses to be dragged inside (some teams teach him to pass the post on to the free
safety and stay outside for anything up the sideline), the post is the throw: now it's a
one-on-one inside against the free safety, whom the backside seam has held in the middle. We file
post-wheel as a horizontal stretch because that is its shape: two deep routes, one breaking inside
and one outside, splitting the defenders' areas side to side. Against man coverage it is better
still: the wheel puts a slot receiver or a running back against a nickel or a linebacker who has to
turn and run up the sideline with him.

### Scissors

[**Scissors**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-scissors) is post-wheel's two-high cousin. The
outside receiver still runs a post, but the inside receiver runs a corner route instead of a wheel,
so their paths cross at 10 to 12 yards like the blades of a pair of scissors. It is read inside
first: the post.

::: {#cell-fig-scissors .cell execution_count=20}
``` {.python .cell-code}
p = Play(spread(), quarters(extra={"SS": (10.5, 6.6), "FS": (10.5, -6.6)}), los=LOS, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(3.0)
route_to(p, "Z", (9.3, 15.0), (19.5, 5.0))
route_to(p, "Y", (8.5, 9.0), (18.5, 18.6))
rb_n = swing(p, -1)
p.drop("NB", (8.5, 10.0))
p.drop("FS", (15.0, -8.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -5.0))
p.drop("LCB", (15.0, -16.0))
p.highlight("SS", "RCB")
fld = plate(p, nums=[(1, (21.2, 3.4)), (2, (20.0, 20.6)), (3, rb_n)],
            ghosts=[[(-0.7, -15.0), (11.3, -15.0), (11.3, -5.0)], [(-1.5, -9.0), (5.0, -9.0), (5.2, -7.0)]],
            stretch="Horizontal stretch: safety and corner",
            keys=["route", "ghost", "drop", "react", "num", "ring", "ltg"])
branch(fld, p, [(10.5, 6.6), (13.4, 7.8), (16.2, 14.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
branch(fld, p, [(7.5, 16.0), (11.0, 16.2), (15.6, 11.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
point_to(fld, p, (17.6, -1.0), (12.0, 12.4), "the blades cross\nat about 12 yards", color=OD)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Scissors to the offense's right against Quarters. Z runs a post, Y a corner route; their paths cross at about 12 yards. The two ringed defenders both lose their leverage (dashed): the strong safety, who starts inside Y and carries him when he goes vertical, has to cross the field outside to follow the corner route; the cornerback, who starts outside Z, has to cross inside to follow the post. Their paths cross too, a rub at depth. The progression: (1) the post, inside the cornerback and away from the safety; (2) the corner route, if the safety passes Y on and stays inside; (3) the back, checking down on the left.](04-04-dropback-concepts_files/figure-html/fig-scissors-output-1.svg){#fig-scissors}
:::
:::


Scissors beats Quarters by turning its leverage inside out. In Quarters, as you saw with dagger, the
safety reads the inside receiver from *inside* leverage and carries him if he goes vertical, and
the cornerback plays the outside receiver almost man-to-man from *outside* leverage. Each defender
starts on the side of his receiver that the receiver is least likely to break toward. Scissors
sends both receivers the other way. Y goes vertical, so the safety carries him, and then Y breaks
*outside*: the safety has to cross the field toward the sideline, through Z's path, from the wrong
side. Z breaks *inside* on the post: the cornerback has to cross inside, through Y's path, from the
wrong side. Both defenders lose their leverage at once, and the crossing paths add a rub at depth.
Against man coverage the same crossing makes it a man-beater, too.

### Yankee

[**Yankee**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yankee) is a two-man deep shot. One receiver runs a
post from one side; the other runs a deep over route, a crosser at about 18 to 22 yards, from the
other side. Both routes finish in the deep middle, one above the single deep safety and one in
front of him. It is usually run off
[play-action](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-play-action), with a fake handoff to freeze the
linebackers, and with [max protection](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-max-protect), seven or eight
blockers, because both routes take three seconds or more to develop.

Why does it work? The run fake does half the job. Linebackers are taught to stop the run first,
so they step forward when they see a handoff, and that step takes them out of the path of the deep
over, which crosses behind them at a depth no underneath defender can reach. The other half is a
high-low on the one man left: the free safety in the middle of the field can sink to take away the
post or come forward to take away the over, not both. The post keeps him honest, and the over is
thrown where nobody else can reach it: in front of the deep-third cornerback, who can't leave his
deep outside area, and behind linebackers who have just stepped toward a handoff. Sean McVay's Rams made yankee one of their
signature shot plays of the late 2010s (the Rams often ran it from three-receiver sets with jet
motion), Kyle Shanahan's 49ers ran it too, and it now appears in most NFL playbooks that come from
the Shanahan and McVay family of offenses.[^yankee] The price is the
protection: with seven or eight blockers, only two or three receivers go out, so if the safety
plays it perfectly the quarterback has very little to throw to. How play-action works,
and why the fake works even when the run game doesn't, belongs to
[Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd).

## Tags and route conversions

Fourteen concepts sounds like a lot, but a real playbook has many more, and most of the extras
aren't new concepts at all. They are the same concepts with a word added. A
[tag](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tag) is a word added to a play call that changes one
player's assignment and leaves everyone else's alone. "Mesh" tells all five receivers what to do;
"Mesh, Z-wheel" keeps mesh intact except for Z, who runs a wheel instead of his corner route. Tags
let a play-caller adjust a concept to a defense's habits (a cornerback who jumps corner routes, a
safety who cheats toward the crossers) without teaching a new play.

The second tool is subtler, and it explains how one call can be right against several coverages.
A [**route conversion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-route-conversion) is a rule built into a
route that changes it according to the coverage the receiver sees. The receiver doesn't wait for
the quarterback to tell him; he reads the defense himself, usually the safeties, and the
quarterback, reading the same thing, knows where he will be.

::: {#cell-fig-conversion .cell execution_count=22}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.7))
for ax, one_high in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    off = [O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 8.0), O("C", "C", LINE_D, 0.0)]
    if one_high:

    if one_high:
```

You've already met the most important conversion. The
[option route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-option-route) of
[Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd), which some systems call the *choice route*,
is a conversion with two branches: against man, break away from the defender's leverage; against
zone, sit in the hole. Others are everywhere in this chapter. The smash corner route goes to depth
over a squatting Cover 2 cornerback and flattens under a bailing Cover 3 one. The levels and mesh
crossers keep running against man and settle against zone. The dagger dig sits down in a window
against zone and keeps crossing against man. And the Y-cross, the Air Raid's most
conversion-heavy route, keeps running toward the far sideline against Cover 3 and man, and sits
down in the window against two deep safeties or a robber lurking in the middle.

One caution about names while we're here. Teams name the same concept differently (you've already
met flood and sail, and levels as the Colts' "Dig"), and some reuse a name for a different concept.
The *shape* is what to learn; a name only tells you what one team calls it.

The Patriots of the Tom Brady era were the model of an offense built on conversions. Their
Erhardt-Perkins system (named for Ron Erhardt and Ray Perkins, who coached together on New England's
staff in the 1970s, and carried forward by Bill Parcells to Bill Belichick and Josh McDaniels) named
whole concepts with short words, so a quarterback could call them at the line.[^ep] It also gave
its slot receivers wide freedom to read and adjust their routes after the snap: the option routes of
Troy Brown, Deion Branch, Wes Welker and Julian Edelman, which broke one way against man and sat
down against zone, were a staple of the Brady years.[^option] That's why New England's
passing game seemed to have an answer for every defense without a thousand plays: the same few
concepts, each with branches. The system's history and its rivals are in
[Offensive Systems and Languages](04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, the receiver runs the route drawn on the play art, whatever the defense does, and
you press a button for the one you want. In the NFL, a large share of routes are conditional: the
receiver converts the route against the coverage, the quarterback has to read the same thing and
throw to where the receiver *will* be, and a mismatch between their reads is one of the commonest
causes of an interception that looks, on the broadcast, like the quarterback threw to nobody. When
an announcer says a receiver and quarterback "weren't on the same page," that's usually what
happened: one of them saw man and the other saw zone.
:::

## The quarterback's side: one clock for every concept

Each plate in this chapter carried a progression, and they all follow the same pattern. That
pattern is the real skill of dropback passing, so it is worth spelling out.

**Before the snap**, the quarterback identifies the shell (one high safety or two), checks the
leverage of the defenders over the receivers in the concept, and asks the question every concept
poses: *who is the defender in conflict, and where is he?* If the concept is called to both sides,
as smash often is, this is when he picks the side. And if what he sees is wrong for the call (a
zone-beater against a defense that is plainly in man, say), many offenses let him change it: the
play comes in as a pair of concepts, or with a
[check-with-me](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-check-with-me), and he picks at the line
([The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)). The pre-snap picture is
still only a hypothesis; the first step of the safeties after the snap confirms or breaks it
([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)).

If the defense shows a blitz, he checks the protection
([Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd)). Every dropback concept carries its own pressure
answer: if the defense brings one more rusher than the protection can block, the concept's quickest
route becomes the [hot route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route), the throw that has to come
out before the free rusher arrives. On drive and mesh that is a shallow crosser, which is open
almost at once against a blitz; on smash, flood or dagger it is usually the shortest route (the
hitch, the flat) or the back releasing from the backfield.

**At the snap**, his eyes go to the conflict defender, not to a receiver. His drop is timed so
that the first read is ready as his back foot lands: on smash, the corner route breaks as he hits
the bottom of his drop; on dagger, the dig arrives a beat later, which is why dagger takes a deeper
drop or a hitch step.

**After the first look**, he moves to the next read with his feet as well as his eyes. Each
*hitch step*, a short step up into the pocket, resets his feet for the next throw. A typical dropback
progression gets two or three looks before the rush arrives; the last is the
[checkdown](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown), the short throw to a back that keeps the
play from losing yards. As [Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd) showed with FTN's
charting, more than half of all throws go to the first read, and those are the quickest and most
valuable: the concept is at its best when its first answer is right.

**The order of the looks** follows the two rhythms from the start of the chapter: high to low
on most vertical stretches, low to high when a shallow crosser wins early or not at all, and on a
long third down, the route that reaches the line to gain first.

The table gathers the fourteen concepts, the family each belongs to, the defender it puts in a bind
and the coverage it's built to beat. The last column is the subject of
[What Beats What](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd), which pairs concepts
with coverages in detail; how each coverage defends these concepts is in Part 6, beginning with
[Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) and, for four verticals,
[The Cover 3 Family](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd).

| Concept | Family | Defender in conflict | Built to beat | Typical progression |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Smash | Vertical stretch | Cornerback | Cover 2 | corner → hitch → back |
| Flood (sail) | Vertical, three levels | Curl-flat defender | Cover 3 | sail → flat (go if the corner sits) |
| Curl-flat | Triangle | Curl-flat and hook defenders | Cover 3, zone | curl → flat → hook |
| Levels | Vertical stretch | Hook linebacker | Zone | dig → in → back |
| Drive | Vertical; also a man-beater | Middle linebacker | Zone and man | shallow → dig → back |
| Shallow cross | Vertical; also a man-beater | Middle linebacker | Zone and man | shallow → dig or sit → back |
| Dagger | Vertical stretch | Safety, then the cornerback | Two-high (Quarters, Cover 2) | seam → dig → back |
| Y-cross | Vertical, three levels | Far curl-flat defender | Cover 3, man | cross → flat → back |
| Mesh | Man-beater | Man defenders on the crossers | Man (Cover 1, Cover 0) | corner → crossers → back |
| Angle (Texas) | Man-beater | Linebacker covering the back | Man | angle → seam |
| Four verticals | Horizontal, deep | Free safety | Cover 3, Cover 2 | seam away from the safety → back |
| Post-wheel | Horizontal, deep | Cornerback and curl-flat defender | Match Cover 3, man | wheel → post → back |
| Scissors | Horizontal, deep | Safety and cornerback | Quarters | post → corner → back |
| Yankee | Vertical, deep | Free safety | One-high | post → over → outlet |

: The fourteen dropback concepts at a glance. "Built to beat" is the concept's best matchup, not its only one. {#tbl-concepts}

Two honest limits on this table. First, you usually **can't tell these concepts apart before the
snap**, and that is by design: smash, flood and post-wheel all start as a slot and an outside
receiver on one side, and an offense that tipped which one was coming would be easy to defend.
What you *can* predict before the snap is the family, from the shell (two-high invites smash,
dagger and scissors; one-high invites flood, four verticals, post-wheel and yankee; man invites
mesh and the angle route) and from the down and distance. The concept itself reveals itself in the
first two seconds, when the routes break. Second, nobody publishes how often each concept is
called. Public play-by-play records where the ball went, not what was drawn; the Big Data Bowl
tracking data at the end of this chapter charts each receiver's route, which is enough to find
concepts by their route combinations if you want to count them yourself.

## Film room

The concepts above are in almost every NFL playbook. A few teams built an identity on them, and watching
those teams is the fastest way to learn to see the concepts at game speed.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Texas Tech 2007–2008"}
**Mesh and Y-cross, rep after rep.** Mike Leach's Texas Tech teams were the Air Raid at full
volume. In 2007, quarterback Graham Harrell threw for 5,705 yards and redshirt freshman receiver Michael
Crabtree caught 134 passes for 1,962 yards and 22 touchdowns; Crabtree won the Biletnikoff Award as
the nation's best receiver that season and again in 2008.[^ttu] Nearly all of it came out of the
same small menu of concepts drawn in this chapter: mesh, shallow cross, Y-cross and four verticals,
from wide 2x2 and trips formations with enormous splits between the offensive linemen.

**What to notice on the tape:** the mesh point, two crossers passing over the center close enough to
touch, and a defender losing a step as he goes around; Harrell's eyes on the curl-flat defender on
Y-cross, and the ball arriving as the crosser came into the window; and how *few* different plays
there were. The defense knew what was coming, and it didn't matter, because the offense had run
each concept thousands of times against every look.

**One game to find:** Texas Tech's 39–33 win over No. 1 Texas on November 1, 2008, the school's
first win over a top-ranked team. Trailing 33–32 with 1:29 left, Harrell drove the Red Raiders 62
yards in six plays, and Crabtree caught the winning touchdown at the sideline with one second
left.[^ttutx] The final drive is famous; the rest of the game is the small menu at work.

Leach's former quarterback Kliff Kingsbury later brought the same concepts to the NFL as the Arizona
Cardinals' head coach (2019–2022), and in 2026 joined Sean McVay's Rams staff as assistant head
coach.[^kingsbury]
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams 2018"}
**Yankee and the play-action shot.** In Sean McVay's second season, the Rams went 13–3 and reached
Super Bowl LIII, where they lost to New England 13–3. Jared Goff threw for 4,688 yards and 32
touchdowns.[^rams] Their passing game ran on a single foundation: line up in the same formation with
three receivers, run outside-zone handoffs out of it, and throw play-action shots from the same look,
yankee among them. On throws of 20 yards or more in the air, the Rams averaged about +0.77 EPA
per attempt, third-best in the league, against a league average of about +0.37.[^deep18]

**What to notice on the tape:** the linebackers' first step on the run fake, *toward* the line;
the deep over crossing behind them at 18 to 20 yards; and the free safety in the middle, who has to
decide between the over in front of him and the post behind him. Goff often had only two routes to
choose from, and his decision was made by one defender.

**One game to find:** the Rams' 54–51 win over the Chiefs on Monday night, November 19, 2018, in
Los Angeles, when Goff threw for 413 yards and four touchdowns and Mahomes for 478 yards and six.[^mnf18]
Both offenses' play-action and deep shots are on display; it is the companion game for the next film
room too.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs 2018"}
**Four verticals with a 50-touchdown quarterback.** In Patrick Mahomes's first season as the starter
he threw for 5,097 yards and 50 touchdowns and was named the league's MVP. Andy Reid's offense threw
deep more than almost anyone: 15% of the Chiefs' attempts traveled 20 yards or more in the air (fifth
in the league; the league average was 12%), and those throws were worth about +0.75 EPA each, fourth
best.[^kc18] With Tyreek Hill's speed outside and Travis Kelce running up the seam, vertical routes
made every deep defender declare early, which is the idea four verticals is built on.

**What to notice on the tape:** the deep defenders' first steps. With Hill on the outside, cornerbacks
bailed at the snap, which opened everything underneath; with Kelce on a seam, the middle safety had to
choose. Watch the seam routes for a conversion, bending or staying straight as the receiver reads the
safeties, and Mahomes moving the safety with his eyes before throwing the other way. The November 19
game against the Rams (above) is the place to start: Mahomes threw six touchdowns and three
interceptions, a good lesson in what deep shots cost as well as what they pay.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: name the concept"}
**Before the snap**

- **Find the shell.** One deep safety or two? Smash, dagger and scissors are two-high beaters;
  flood, post-wheel and yankee feast on one-high; four verticals is built for Cover 3 and still
  splits Cover 2's safeties. (Can't see the safeties on the TV angle? See
  [How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd).)
- **Man or zone?** Pressed corners, a defender following a motion man across the formation: think
  man, and think mesh, rubs and the angle route.
- **Check the situation.** On third-and-long, expect a concept with a route past the line to gain;
  on third-and-short against man, expect crossers and rubs. You are predicting a *family*, not a
  name: from the same formation, smash, flood and post-wheel look identical until the routes break.

**On the replay** (the end-zone camera or the skycam is best)

- **Find the defender in conflict first.** Who stood between the routes on the side the ball went
  to? What did he do? The ball usually went to the receiver he didn't take.
- **Then name the stretch by where the routes were *around him* when the ball came out.** One above
  and one below him: a vertical stretch (even if the routes crossed on the way there, as in drive or
  Y-cross). One on each side: horizontal. Three around two defenders: a triangle. No zone defender
  to stretch at all, with receivers running away from men chasing them through traffic: a
  man-beater. Then name the concept.
- **Count the time.** A dropback concept takes about "one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two,
  one-thousand-three." If the ball is out before "two," it was the quick game.

**For your prediction log** ([How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
on each third-and-medium, write the shell you see and the concept family you expect (two-high:
smash or dagger; one-high: flood or a deep shot; man: mesh or rubs). Check yourself on the replay.
:::

**The call sheet for this down has smash and dagger, both to the right. Which one should the
offense run against this picture, and why not the other?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Dagger.** Two high safeties, yes, but this isn't the Cover 2 that smash was built for. Cover 2's
safeties sit 12 to 14 yards deep and wide, and its cornerbacks squat at five yards. Here the safeties
are low and over the slots and the cornerbacks are off: that's the Quarters look, where each safety
reads the slot receiver in front of him.

Against Quarters, smash runs into trouble on both routes. The corner route is the slot going vertical
and then outside, which is exactly what the safety is reading: he carries it from inside, and the
cornerback, playing deep and outside over the hitch, is above it, so the corner route is
bracketed. The hitch underneath is open against an off cornerback, but it's five or six yards on
third-and-9: short of the sticks, and it needs yards after the catch.

Dagger turns the same safety rule against him. Y's seam takes the safety deep; the nickel and the
Mike sink under it; and the dig comes in behind them against a cornerback playing from outside, at
15 yards, past the line to gain. What would make the quarterback come off it? A safety who doesn't
carry the seam (then throw the seam), or a rotation at the snap to one deep safety (then the seam
attacks the middle safety, and the dig crosses under him).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Mesh.** Everything here says man coverage: pressed cornerbacks, a defender over every receiver,
a single safety deep, and, the clincher, a nickel who followed H across the formation and back on the
motion. Zone defenders don't travel with a motion man; man defenders do
([Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)).

Against man, the zone-beaters lose their point. Flood's three levels stretch a curl-flat defender who
doesn't exist; each receiver just has a defender following him. Four verticals is a better man answer
but needs three seconds and a receiver who can beat a pressed cornerback deep, which is a big ask on
third-and-3. Mesh is built for this: the two crossers run at five or six yards, past the line to
gain, and the defenders on H and Y have to fight through each other's traffic. One of the crossers
usually comes free within about two seconds, running away from his man.

How does the offense act on what it saw? If the play called in the huddle was flood, a quarterback
with a check-with-me or a paired call can switch to mesh at the line; that's exactly what motion is
for. What should still worry him? The Mike linebacker. In Cover 1, the defender not assigned to
anyone often sits in the middle as a [robber](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-robber), exactly where
the crossers meet. The quarterback has to find him before the snap and throw the crosser running
away from him.
:::
:::

**Which family is it, who is the defender in conflict, what coverage does it want, and in what
order should the quarterback read it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A vertical stretch (a high-low) of the free safety, built to beat one-high coverage, read high to
low: the post, then the dig, then the back.** Both routes break toward the middle, which can
make it look like a horizontal stretch or a crossing man-beater. Ask where the routes are *around
the key defender* when the ball comes out: the post is
above the free safety, heading for the deep middle he guards, and the dig is below him, crossing at
14 yards, above the linebackers. One defender, two depths.

That makes it yankee's logic from one side of the formation, without the run fake: if the safety
sinks for the post, the dig comes open in front of him; if he comes up for the dig, the post is
behind him. Against two deep safeties, the middle is open and the post has nobody to stretch, so an
offense would rather have this against a one-high shell (or with a conversion that bends the post
away from a second safety).
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- A **pass concept** is a set of routes built to work together, usually by putting one or two
  defenders in a bind; it has a name so the whole offense can learn and call it as a unit, from any
  formation.
- Concepts come in **four families**, named by where the routes are around the key defender when
  the ball comes out: **vertical stretches** (one above him, one below: smash, flood, levels, drive,
  shallow cross, dagger, Y-cross, yankee), **horizontal stretches** (one on each side, deep: four
  verticals, post-wheel, scissors), **triangles** (three receivers around two defenders: curl-flat,
  snag) and **man-beaters** (traffic and leverage against man defenders: mesh, the angle route).
- Each concept is built to beat certain coverages: smash, dagger and scissors attack **two-high**;
  flood, post-wheel and yankee attack **one-high**; four verticals is built for Cover 3 and still
  splits Cover 2; mesh and the angle route attack **man**. That is why the quarterback's pre-snap
  read starts with the safeties.
- The quarterback reads **the defender in conflict, not the receivers**, usually high to low (low
  to high when a shallow crosser leads), and his progression runs on his feet: the first read as his
  back foot lands, the next on a hitch step, the checkdown last.
- **Rub routes** beat man coverage by making defenders run through traffic; a receiver who deliberately
  blocks a defender more than a yard downfield, until the pass is touched, commits **offensive pass
  interference**.
- **Tags** change one route in a concept; **route conversions** let a route change itself by coverage,
  so one call can be right against several defenses. The **intermediate middle** of the field is the
  most valuable place to throw, and most of these concepts exist to get the ball there.

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"}
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
player_play = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/player_play.csv")
routes = player_play.dropna(subset=["routeRan"])

# four verticals: at least four receivers on GO routes on the same play
gos = routes[routes["routeRan"] == "GO"].groupby(["gameId", "playId"]).size()
verts = gos[gos >= 4].reset_index()[["gameId", "playId"]]

# mesh-like: two or more crossing routes on the same play, thrown to a crosser
cross = routes[routes["routeRan"] == "CROSS"].groupby(["gameId", "playId"]).size()
mesh = cross[cross >= 2].reset_index()[["gameId", "playId"]]
mesh = mesh.merge(plays[["gameId", "playId", "passResult", "pff_manZone"]], on=["gameId", "playId"])
mesh_vs_man = mesh[mesh["pff_manZone"] == "Man"]

g, pl = verts.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 1.2, 2.4, 3.2])   # snap, release, safety's choice, catch
```
